nameStory: The black ash gets its name from its distinctively dark, almost black bark that becomes deeply furrowed with age. Unlike its lighter-colored cousins like white ash, this tree's somber bark makes it easy to spot in the forest. The scientific name Fraxinus comes from the Latin word for ash tree, while 'nigra' means black.
description: Black ash is a medium to large deciduous tree that can reach 40-60 feet tall in New England's wetlands. It has a slender trunk with distinctive dark, furrowed bark and compound leaves made up of 7-11 leaflets arranged along a central stem. This moisture-loving tree often grows in swampy areas where few other large trees can thrive, creating distinctive wetland forests. Its crown tends to be narrow and open compared to other ash species.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Dark gray to nearly black bark with deep, diamond-shaped furrows and scaly ridges. The bark feels rough and corky to the touch, much darker than other ash species.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Compound leaves with 7-11 narrow, pointed leaflets arranged opposite each other along a central stem. The leaflets lack stalks (sessile) except for the terminal one, and feel thin and papery compared to white ash.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Slender trunk with a narrow, open crown. Often grows in dense stands in swampy areas, sometimes with multiple trunks from the base in wet conditions.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Paddle-shaped winged seeds (samaras) that hang in clusters. The wing extends down both sides of the seed body, unlike white ash where it's only at the tip.

idTips.label: Buds
idTips.description: Dark brown to black winter buds that are smaller and more pointed than white ash. The buds feel sticky when crushed and have a distinctive bitter smell.

habitat: Black ash thrives in New England's wettest spots - swamps, stream banks, lake shores, and poorly drained bottomlands. You'll often find it growing alongside red maple, American elm, and various willows in areas that flood seasonally. It prefers rich, organic soils that stay moist to wet year-round, from sea level up to about 1,500 feet elevation.

seasonality.spring: Small, inconspicuous purple flowers appear before the leaves emerge in April-May. New leaves unfurl as bright green compound leaves that are quite distinctive when backlit by spring sun.
seasonality.summer: Full foliage shows the characteristic 7-11 leaflet compound leaves. The narrow crown provides dappled shade, and winged seeds begin developing in drooping clusters.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn yellow to brown, often dropping earlier than other trees. The distinctive winged seeds mature and fall, carpeting wet areas beneath the trees.
seasonality.winter: Dark, furrowed bark and narrow branching pattern are most visible. Small, dark buds and persistent seed wings on the ground help confirm identification.

funFact: Black ash wood is so perfectly suited for basket making that when you pound a log with a sledgehammer, the annual growth rings will separate into thin, flexible strips that Native Americans and craftspeople have used for centuries to weave baskets - no other North American tree does this!
confusionNotes: Most often confused with white ash, but black ash has much darker bark, grows in wet areas (white ash prefers well-drained sites), and its leaflets lack individual stalks. Remember: 'Black ash, black bark, boggy ground' versus 'White ash, light bark, well-drained dirt.'
contextualKnowledge: Black ash faces an existential crisis from the invasive emerald ash borer, which threatens to eliminate virtually all ash species from North American forests within decades. This is particularly devastating for Native American communities who depend on black ash for traditional basket making, as no other tree species can substitute for its unique wood properties.
compareHints: Black ash differs from white ash by its preference for wet habitats, darker bark, and leaflets that lack individual stalks (sessile). Compared to green ash, black ash has more leaflets (7-11 vs 5-9), darker bark, and strictly prefers wetland habitats rather than the more adaptable green ash that tolerates various soil conditions.

relatedSpecies.distinction: White ash differs from black ash by preferring drier, upland sites (black ash loves wet areas) and having leaflets with short stalks, while black ash leaflets attach directly to the main stem.
Green ash differs from white ash by its fuzzy, green-tinged leaf undersides (white ash has smooth, whitish undersides) and its greater tolerance for wet soils.
European ash differs from our native ashes primarily in its black, velvety winter buds - white ash has brown buds, green ash has smaller brown buds, and black ash has dark but pointed buds.
